questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with hypopigmented anaesthetic patches on his trunk and thickened ulnar nerves bilaterally. Slit skin smear is negative. Skin biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation with lymphocytes and epithelioid cells around dermal nerves but no bacilli. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Borderline tuberculoid (BT) leprosy presents with few hypopigmented anaesthetic patches, asymmetric nerve involvement, and negative SSS. Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation around nerves but bacilli are absent or scanty (BI 0-1+). Lepromatous leprosy would show numerous bacilli and poorly formed granulomas.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman develops tense blisters on normal-appearing skin and mucous membranes. Direct immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposits at the basement membrane zone. ELISA is positive for anti-BP230 antibodies. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most common autoimmune bullous disorder with linear IgG/C3 at BMZ. Anti-BP180 and anti-BP230 are targets. First-line treatment is systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 0.5-1 mg/kg/day). Rituximab is reserved for refractory cases.

questions.q: A 45-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with painless ulcers with undermined edges and satellite lesions on the face. KOH mount shows large spherical yeast cells with broad-based budding. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Blastomyces dermatitidis produces large (8-15 μm) spherical yeast with characteristic broad-based (figure-of-8) budding. It causes North American blastomycosis with skin, lung, and bone involvement. Cryptococcus shows narrow-based budding with capsule; Histoplasma is intracellular.

questions.q: A 22-year-old male presents with painful genital ulcer with ragged, undermined edges and inguinal lymphadenopathy (buboes). Gram stain of the ulcer shows Gram-negative coccobacilli arranged in 'school of fish' pattern. What is the most effective treatment?
questions.exp: Chancroid (Haemophilus ducreyi) presents with painful soft ulcer and suppurative inguinal lymphadenopathy. 'School of fish' pattern on Gram stain is characteristic. Treatment: Azithromycin 1g single dose OR Ceftriaxone 250mg IM single dose OR Ciprofloxacin 500mg BD for 3 days.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman on hydroxychloroquine for SLE develops a fixed drug eruption. She presents with sharply demarcated hyperpigmented oval patch that recurs at the same site on rechallenge. What is the histopathological hallmark?
opts: Basal cell vacuolation with pigment incontinence
questions.exp: Fixed drug eruption histologically shows interface dermatitis with basal cell vacuolation, dyskeratotic keratinocytes, and prominent melanin incontinence (pigment in macrophages in dermis). This explains the residual hyperpigmentation. Acantholysis is seen in pemphigus; subepidermal blisters in BP.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman presents with malar erythema, discoid plaques, photosensitivity, and oral ulcers. ANA is positive at 1:320 (homogeneous pattern). Which antibody, if positive, is most specific for SLE and correlates with disease activity?
questions.exp: Anti-dsDNA antibodies are highly specific for SLE (95-99%) and their titers correlate with disease activity and lupus nephritis. Anti-Sm is also specific for SLE but doesn't correlate with activity. Anti-Ro is associated with neonatal lupus and subacute cutaneous lupus. Anti-histone is seen in drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A 40-year-old farmer presents with painless warty nodule on the dorsum of his hand that slowly enlarged over 6 months. Biopsy shows pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with 'copper penny' (sclerotic bodies) in the dermis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis is caused by dematiaceous fungi (Fonsecaea, Phialophora, Cladosporium). Key histological feature: 'copper penny' or 'Medlar bodies' (sclerotic bodies - golden-brown, thick-walled, septate cells). Mycetoma shows grains/granules; Sporotrichosis shows asteroid bodies.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with annular, erythematous, scaling plaques with central clearing on the trunk. KOH examination reveals septate hyphae. Treatment with topical clotrimazole for 4 weeks fails. What is the next step?
questions.exp: Tinea corporis refractory to topical azoles should be treated with oral antifungals. Terbinafine (allylamine) is fungicidal and first-line for dermatophytoses - 250mg for 2-4 weeks for tinea corporis. It has highest cure rates and lowest relapse rates compared to azoles for dermatophyte infections.

questions.q: A 16-year-old presents with comedones, inflammatory papules, and nodules on the face. He has tried topical benzoyl peroxide and clindamycin for 3 months without improvement. What is the most appropriate next treatment?
questions.exp: For moderate-to-severe inflammatory acne refractory to topical therapy, oral antibiotics (doxycycline 100mg BD) are indicated. Oral isotretinoin is reserved for severe nodulo-cystic acne, acne with scarring, or cases unresponsive to oral antibiotics. The step before isotretinoin is a trial of oral antibiotics.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male smoker presents with a pearly papule with rolled edges and central ulceration on the nose. Dermoscopy shows arborizing blood vessels. What is the most common histological subtype?
questions.exp: Nodular BCC is the most common subtype (60-80%), presenting as a pearly papule with telangiectasias and central ulceration (rodent ulcer). Dermoscopy shows arborizing (tree-like) vessels, blue-grey ovoid nests, and ulceration. Morpheaform is the most aggressive subtype with ill-defined borders.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and telangiectasias. ANA shows anticentromere pattern. HRCT chest is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Limited cutaneous SSc (CREST syndrome) is characterized by: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia. Anti-centromere antibodies are specific for lcSSc. Skin involvement is limited to face, hands, and feet. Pulmonary hypertension is a late complication. dcSSc has anti-Scl-70 (topoisomerase I).

questions.q: A neonate develops blisters at sites of minor trauma. EM shows blistering below the lamina densa. Immunofluorescence mapping shows absent type VII collagen. What is the most likely inheritance pattern?
questions.exp: Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB) is caused by mutations in COL7A1 (type VII collagen). Recessive DEB (Hallopeau-Siemens type) is the most severe form with complete absence of type VII collagen, mitten deformity of hands, esophageal strictures, and increased risk of SCC. Dominant DEB has reduced but present type VII collagen.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man presents with erosions and flaccid blisters on the trunk and scalp. Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG deposits giving 'chicken wire' pattern. Which antigen is targeted?
questions.exp: Pemphigus vulgaris targets desmoglein 3 (mucosal dominant) and desmoglein 1 (mucocutaneous type). The 'chicken wire' or 'fishnet' pattern on DIF is characteristic of pemphigus (intercellular IgG deposits). BP180 (BPAG2) and BP230 (BPAG1) are targets in bullous pemphigoid with linear basement membrane deposits.

questions.q: A 28-year-old pregnant woman in second trimester develops intensely pruritic urticarial papules and plaques in striae distensae of abdomen sparing the umbilicus. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: PEP (Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy), previously PUPPP, is the most common dermatosis of pregnancy. It begins in abdominal striae and characteristically spares the umbilicus. Occurs in third trimester, primigravidas. DIF is negative. Pemphigoid gestationis starts periumbilically, has linear C3 on DIF, and targets BP180.

questions.q: A 20-year-old presents with silvery-white scaling plaques on the elbows, knees, and scalp with nail pitting. Auspitz sign is positive. Which cell type is primarily responsible for the pathogenesis?
questions.exp: Psoriasis is primarily driven by Th17 cells secreting IL-17A, IL-17F, and IL-22, which stimulate keratinocyte proliferation. The IL-23/Th17 axis is central to pathogenesis. This explains why IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab) and IL-23 inhibitors (guselkumab) are highly effective. Th2 predominates in atopic dermatitis.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male develops a painless indurated ulcer on the penis with clean base and indurated edges. VDRL is non-reactive but TPHA is positive. What should be done next?
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (chancre) may have non-reactive VDRL in early infection (window period). Dark-field microscopy of serous discharge from the ulcer to demonstrate Treponema pallidum is the most direct diagnostic test for primary syphilis. TPHA positivity supports syphilis diagnosis. FTA-ABS is confirmatory but dark-field is more specific for active infection.

questions.q: A 35-year-old woman on methotrexate for psoriasis develops megaloblastic anemia and oral ulcers. She was not given folic acid supplementation. At what step does methotrexate primarily act?
questions.exp: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), preventing conversion of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, depleting reduced folate stores needed for purine and thymidylate synthesis. This inhibits DNA synthesis in rapidly dividing cells. Folic acid 5mg/week (not on methotrexate day) reduces side effects. Folinic acid is the antidote in toxicity.

questions.q: A 55-year-old presents with urticaria and angioedema after taking ACE inhibitor for hypertension. The swelling involves lips and tongue and does not respond to antihistamines or epinephrine. What mediator is primarily responsible?
questions.exp: ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema is bradykinin-mediated. ACE normally degrades bradykinin; ACE inhibition leads to bradykinin accumulation causing vasodilation and increased vascular permeability. It doesn't respond to antihistamines or epinephrine (which target histamine-mediated angioedema). Treatment: FFP, icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist), or C1 esterase inhibitor concentrate.

questions.q: A 40-year-old farmer presents with painless, slowly progressive swelling of the foot with multiple sinuses discharging black grains. What is the most common cause in India?
questions.exp: Mycetoma (Madura foot) in India is most commonly caused by Madurella mycetomatis (eumycetoma - black grains). Actinomadura madurae causes actinomycetoma with white-to-yellow grains. Nocardia causes fine white/yellow grains. Madurella mycetomatis grains are black due to melanin. Treatment: surgical debridement + itraconazole or voriconazole.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with well-defined, hyperpigmented patches with fine adherent scales on the chest. Wood's lamp shows yellow-green fluorescence. KOH shows 'spaghetti and meatballs' appearance. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Topical selenium sulfide or ketoconazole shampoo
questions.exp: Pityriasis versicolor is caused by Malassezia furfur (Pityrosporum orbiculare). KOH shows hyphae and spores ('spaghetti and meatballs'). Wood's lamp shows yellow-green fluorescence. First-line: topical selenium sulfide 2.5% lotion OR ketoconazole shampoo applied to affected areas. Terbinafine is not effective against Malassezia as it lacks ergosterol-dependent steps that terbinafine targets.

questions.q: A 45-year-old male presents with a painless, slowly enlarging, flesh-colored plaque on the chest wall with 'dermafibrosarcoma protuberans' on biopsy. CD34 is positive. What chromosomal abnormality is characteristic?
questions.exp: DFSP (Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans) is characterized by t(17;22) translocation creating COL1A1-PDGFB fusion gene. CD34 positivity distinguishes it from dermatofibroma (CD34-). Imatinib (tyrosine kinase inhibitor) is used for metastatic/unresectable DFSP as it targets PDGFR-β. Treatment is wide local excision with Mohs surgery preferred.

questions.q: A 72-year-old presents with palpable purpura on lower limbs, arthralgia, and hematuria. Biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA deposits. Serum IgA is elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: IgA vasculitis (HSP) is the most common systemic vasculitis in children but can occur in adults. The tetrad: palpable purpura (lower limbs), arthritis, abdominal pain, renal involvement (IgA nephropathy). Defining feature: perivascular IgA deposits on DIF. Elevated serum IgA. Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis has positive cryoglobulins and is associated with HCV.

questions.q: A 30-year-old female presents with facial butterfly rash, joint pains, and pleuritis. She is started on hydroxychloroquine. What is the most important baseline investigation before starting hydroxychloroquine?
questions.exp: Hydroxychloroquine causes dose-dependent retinal toxicity (bull's eye maculopathy) which can be irreversible. Baseline ophthalmological examination (fundoscopy and OCT) is mandatory before starting HCQ, with annual monitoring after 5 years. G6PD deficiency check is needed for dapsone, not HCQ. The safe daily dose is <5mg/kg/day.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base along the T5 dermatome. The lesions are painful and preceded by a burning sensation for 2 days. Tzanck smear shows multinucleated giant cells. What is the treatment of choice?
opts: Oral acyclovir 800mg 5 times daily for 7 days
questions.exp: Herpes zoster is treated with oral acyclovir 800mg 5 times daily for 7 days. Valacyclovir 1g TDS for 7 days is an equivalent and more convenient alternative. Famciclovir 500mg TDS for 7 days is also used. Topical acyclovir is not recommended for zoster. Treatment should be started within 72 hours of rash onset to reduce PHN risk.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male presents with an asymmetric, multicolored (brown, black, red, white) pigmented lesion on the back measuring 8mm with irregular borders. Dermoscopy shows atypical pigment network, regression structures, and blue-white veil. What is the most appropriate management?
questions.exp: Clinically suspicious pigmented lesion should undergo excisional biopsy with 2mm margins for diagnosis. This provides complete tissue for Breslow thickness measurement, which guides definitive wide excision margins and SLNB decision. Punch biopsy risks sampling error and incomplete staging. SLNB is considered after histological confirmation in Breslow >1mm tumors.

questions.q: A 20-year-old male develops a painless ulcer on the shaft of penis after sexual exposure 3 weeks ago. The ulcer has clean base, indurated edges, and is non-tender. Inguinal lymphadenopathy is rubbery and non-tender. RPR is reactive (1:16). What is the first-line treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose
questions.exp: Primary syphilis is treated with benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM as a single dose. This is the drug of choice. Doxycycline 100mg BD for 14 days is used in penicillin-allergic patients. Azithromycin 2g single dose is an alternative but not recommended due to emerging resistance. Ceftriaxone is also an alternative but not first-line.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman undergoes Mohs micrographic surgery for a basal cell carcinoma on her nose. What is the main advantage of Mohs surgery over wide local excision?
opts: Highest cure rate with maximum tissue conservation
questions.exp: Mohs micrographic surgery allows 100% margin assessment (en face horizontal frozen sections) while minimizing tissue removal. It achieves 5-year cure rates of 99% for primary BCC and 95% for recurrent BCC - superior to any other technique. Indicated for tumors at high-risk sites (nose, ears, eyelids), recurrent tumors, aggressive subtypes (morpheaform), and large tumors.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with lepromatous leprosy. He develops fever, painful nerve enlargement, and new hypopigmented patches 3 months after starting multidrug therapy. What is this reaction called and how is it managed?
opts: Type 1 reaction (reversal reaction) - managed with prednisolone
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction is a delayed hypersensitivity reaction occurring in borderline leprosy (BT, BB, BL) during MDT. Features: upgrading of patches, acute neuritis, edema of hands/feet. Treatment: prednisolone 40-60mg/day tapered over 3-6 months; MDT is continued. Type 2 (ENL) occurs in LL/BL with immune complex deposits; treated with thalidomide or prednisolone.

questions.q: A 35-year-old male with HIV (CD4 count 50 cells/μL) develops multiple pigmented papules and plaques on the face, trunk, and palate. Biopsy shows spindle cell proliferation with slit-like vascular spaces and extravasated red blood cells. What is the causative agent?
questions.exp: AIDS-related Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 (KSHV - Kaposi Sarcoma Herpesvirus). It presents with violaceous patches, plaques, and nodules on skin, mucosa, and viscera. CD4 <200 is a risk factor. Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular channels, extravasated RBCs, and plasma cells. Treatment: ART + chemotherapy (liposomal doxorubicin, paclitaxel).

questions.q: A 30-year-old develops an acute urticarial reaction within 30 minutes of penicillin injection. Skin prick test with penicilloyl-polylysine (PPL) is positive. What is the mechanism of this reaction?
questions.exp: Immediate urticaria/anaphylaxis within 60 minutes of drug exposure is Type I (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity. Penicillin-specific IgE binds to mast cells; re-exposure causes cross-linking and degranulation releasing histamine. Penicilloyl-polylysine (PPL) is the major determinant for skin testing. Type IV (delayed) causes maculopapular exanthem at 24-72 hours; Type III causes serum sickness at 7-14 days.

questions.q: A 25-year-old male presents with hypopigmented macule on the cheek with decreased sensation to light touch. Nerve biopsy shows foamy macrophages (Virchow cells) laden with bacilli. What is the histopathological finding called and in which type of leprosy is it seen?
opts: Globi within Virchow cells - Lepromatous leprosy
Langerhans giant cells - Borderline tuberculoid leprosy
questions.exp: In lepromatous leprosy (LL), foamy macrophages (Virchow cells/lepra cells) are filled with bacilli arranged in parallel arrays called 'globi'. This occurs due to defective T-cell immunity (Th2 predominance, low CMI). Staining with Fite-Faraco stain shows abundant acid-fast bacilli. Bacillary index (BI) is highest (5-6+) in LL. Tuberculoid leprosy shows well-formed epithelioid granulomas with no bacilli.
